candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — occupational sharps injury reporting/recordkeeping
candidate.educational_objective: Apply federal OSHA recordkeeping rules by recording a work-related contaminated needlestick for a Part 1904-covered employer while protecting employee identity and maintaining confidential sharps-injury information.

options.A: If source-patient testing is negative, the injury is not recorded because infection risk has been excluded.
options.B: The injury is recorded only if it later causes lost work time, restricted duty, or a diagnosed bloodborne infection.
options.C: Record the needlestick on the OSHA 300 Log as an injury while protecting the employee's identity, and maintain the required confidential sharps-injury information.
options.D: Keep the event only in employee-health records unless an occupational bloodborne infection is later diagnosed.

candidate.rationale: 29 CFR 1904.8 requires covered employers to record all work-related needlestick injuries and cuts from sharp objects contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material on the OSHA 300 Log as injuries. The employee's name is not entered because these are privacy-concern cases. Under 29 CFR 1910.1030(h)(5), employers required to maintain Part 1904 injury/illness logs must also establish and maintain a sharps-injury log containing specified device, work-area, and incident information in a manner that protects employee confidentiality. Recordability does not depend on source testing, lost work time, or a later infection diagnosis.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Section 1904.8(a) requires recording all work-related contaminated needlesticks/sharps injuries on OSHA 300 as injuries and protects identity; §1910.1030(h)(5) requires a confidential sharps-injury log for employers subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping.
candidate.source_document_title: 29 CFR 1904.8 — Recording criteria for needlestick and sharps injuries; 29 CFR 1910.1030(h)(5) — Sharps injury log
candidate.stem: A nurse employed by a hospital that is required to maintain OSHA injury and illness records sustains a work-related percutaneous injury from a hollow-bore needle contaminated with another person's blood. Which statement about federal OSHA recordkeeping is most accurate?
